summary: This RFC defines a way for the two ends of a Telnet connection to exchange the type of terminal being used. That lets a host treat a user's screen correctly. It was replaced by RFC 930.

plainLanguage.summary: Before you chat, your screen tells the computer what kind of screen it is, so the computer sends things that look right on it.

how does telnet send terminal type
what terminal types does telnet support

what is the telnet terminal type option
subtitle: Let Telnet clients tell servers what kind of terminal they are

tldr.problem: Telnet servers need to know what type of terminal is connected to format data appropriately, but the Telnet protocol had no standard way to exchange this information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 884 defines a Telnet option where the client declares its terminal type (such as VT100 or IBM-3278) as an NVT ASCII string that the server can request or the client can send spontaneously.
tldr.outcome: The terminal type option was replaced by RFC 930 with a more complete specification.

today: RFC 884 was replaced by RFC 930 with improvements.

sections.title: Why Terminal Type Matters
sections.content:
RFC 884 specifies a Telnet option that allows clients to inform servers of their terminal type. Different terminals have different capabilities: some support cursor addressing, color, or special function keys, while others are simple line-oriented displays. Without knowing what terminal is connected, a Telnet server must assume minimal capabilities or send escape sequences that work only on specific terminals.

The option lets a server determine the terminal type and pass that information to its processes or terminal drivers, enabling features like cursor positioning, multiple colors, and special functions that would otherwise be unavailable over a generic Telnet connection. The option integrates smoothly with other Telnet options like BINARY mode.
sections.plainLanguage: When a Telnet connection starts, the terminal sends its type (like "VT100" or "IBM-3278") so the server knows what features it can use.

sections.title: Exchange of Terminal Type Information
sections.content:
The TERMINAL-TYPE option (code 24) uses two negotiation commands: WILL and DO. After the two sides exchange WILL TERMINAL-TYPE and DO TERMINAL-TYPE, the client may send terminal type information either spontaneously or in response to the server's request.

The server uses IAC SB TERMINAL-TYPE SEND IAC SE to request the terminal type, and the client responds with IAC SB TERMINAL-TYPE IS [name] IAC SE where [name] is the terminal name as an NVT ASCII string. Case is not significant. The option allows the client to send multiple names in response to repeated SEND commands, listing from most specific to most generic, allowing the server to use the best match.
sections.plainLanguage: The server asks for the terminal type, and the client answers with a name like "VT100". If the server doesn't understand, it can ask again and the client sends a less specific name.

sections.title: Terminal Type Names
sections.content:
RFC 884 provides suggested terminal type names for three environments. IBM terminals include IBM-3275 through IBM-3279 series models. TOPS-20 environment terminals include DEC models (VT52, VT100), HP models (2621, 2640, 2645), and others like ANN-ARBOR-AMBASSADOR and TEKTRONIX-4025. Unix environment terminals are more numerous: DEC DECWRITER and VT models, HP 26xx series, various data entry and graphics terminals like BITGRAPH, and ASCII terminals like ADM-3.

The RFC notes that the complete list of valid names is maintained in the Assigned Numbers RFC. The type "UNKNOWN" should be used if the terminal type is not known or unlikely to be recognized. The RFC anticipates that additional names will be added over time as new terminals are encountered.
sections.plainLanguage: There are hundreds of possible terminal type names organized by manufacturer: DEC, HP, IBM, Hazeltine, Tektronix, and others. If the server doesn't recognize one, the client can try a more generic name.
